# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
# Review: "Reduced Working Time at Full Pay"

The arithmetic checks out. All per-hour figures equal the output index ÷ 0.8, the sector rows sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees, the weighted mean is 98.7, and the percentage changes in Table 2 are correct. The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. The headline claim that the model is "sector-general" is contradicted by the paper's own data.

## 1. The sector-general conclusion is not supported

**The per-hour "gain" is mechanical.** Output per scheduled hour is the output index ÷ 0.8. Any output index above 80 therefore produces a "gain," so "a gain in every sector" was almost guaranteed and is not evidence. The informative quantity is output itself. In retail and hospitality, output fell by 6.9%.

**For employers, the relevant measure is labour cost per unit of output.** Pay is unchanged, so unit labour cost rises roughly in inverse proportion to output:
- about +7.4% in retail and hospitality (100/93.1),
- about +3.6% in healthcare administration,
- about +1.3% overall.

The pilot's own bargain was "100% of the output." Two sectors, and the sample as a whole, fell short of it.

**The reversions all come from the two weakest sectors.** The paper reports the five reversions without connecting them to sector:

| | Organisations | Continued | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 3 | 50% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 3 | 60% |
| All other sectors | 50 | 50 | 100% |

This is the clearest sector signal in the paper, and it points the other way from the Discussion. The defensible conclusion is that results were strong in knowledge-work sectors and markedly weaker in customer-facing ones. Five and six organisations are also too few to support claims about whole sectors in either direction.

**Coverage was not accounted for.** Seventeen organisations staggered days off to maintain coverage. If coverage was maintained through extra hires, overtime or agency staff, then labour input did not fall by 20%. That bears most directly on retail. Headcount and overtime should be reported.

## 2. The primary outcome is weak

**It is unblinded and subjective.** The output index is completed by managers who were responsible for the pilot, using "whatever output records the organisation held." The Limitations section acknowledges this but then sets it aside.

**Consistency across sectors cannot answer this concern.** The Limitations section argues that consistency makes the result robust. Manager optimism, self-selection and the absence of a control group would bias every sector in the same direction, so consistency is exactly what bias would produce.

**The hours denominator is assumed rather than measured.** If actual hours fell by 10% instead of 20%, the overall per-hour gain drops from +23.4% to about +9.7% (98.7/0.9). Limitation 4 should be quantified, at least for the organisations that did record actual hours.

**Uncertainty is missing.** The paper gives no organisation-level dispersion, no confidence intervals and no monthly trajectory. Only month-six values are reported, although the index was collected monthly.

## 3. Revenue

- **It is nominal.** A 1.4% nominal year-on-year rise during 2023, when inflation was several percent in most economies, is likely a real-terms decline. That is the opposite of "no sign that output was sacrificed."
- **Nine organisations are missing.** Revenue is reported for 52 of 61, and the paper does not say which nine are absent or whether they differ from the rest.
- **The baselines differ.** Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year, while output is compared with the six months immediately before the pilot. This is reasonable for seasonality, but it means the two measures are not directly comparable.
- **The paper's own output index shows a 1.3% decline.** It undercuts "no sign output was sacrificed."

## 4. Wellbeing and retention

**Seasonality.** Revenue is adjusted for season, but sick days and resignations are not. They are compared with the preceding six months. If the baseline covered winter and the pilot covered spring and summer, which is plausible given recruitment in early 2023 plus two months of preparation, a large fall in sickness would be expected regardless.

**Small counts.** About 3.1 resignations per 100 per year across 2,940 staff is roughly 45 a year, or about 23 during the pilot. Employees are also unlikely to resign while an attractive trial is running. The −56% figure is fragile.

**The energy result decays.** Energy rose 0.61 SD at month three and stood at 0.29 SD at month six, roughly halving in three months. The Discussion calls the wellbeing results "consistent" and the Limitations call duration a concern "in either direction." This trend is direct evidence on that question and should be discussed as a possible novelty effect that is fading.

**Survey details are missing.** Response rates and attrition across waves are not reported. "64% rate own productivity higher" has no baseline or comparison and is unverifiable self-report.

## 5. Causal claims in the Discussion

**Fatigue versus process changes.** Fatigue is offered as "the most plausible single explanation," but the evidence presented points elsewhere. Managers described meeting cuts, focus blocks and dropping low-value reporting, and several called the schedule "a forcing device." Those changes could be made without cutting hours. The design cannot separate the two explanations, and the paper should say so rather than favour one.

**Continuation as evidence.** The claim that "continuation is itself evidence" is weak:
- the organisations self-selected as enthusiasts,
- reverting means taking a benefit away from staff, which is costly in morale and retention,
- 38 of the 56 continuers have not yet committed permanently.

**The Limitations conclusion.** The section ends by saying the limitations are "real but unlikely to overturn the main result." That judgement is not argued. Self-selection, no control group, unblinded outcomes and unmeasured hours together could account for much of the effect.

**Attrition before the pilot.** Nine of seventy organisations (13%) withdrew before starting. Their sectors, and whether they foresaw difficulties, should be reported, since this is a further selection step.

## 6. Suggested corrections to the headline claims

| Current | Supportable version |
|---|---|
| "implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%" | "Output fell 1.3% while scheduled hours fell 20%. If actual hours fell by the same amount, output per hour rose about 23%. Actual hours were not measured." |
| "gains in every sector… the model is sector-general" | "Output was near baseline in knowledge-work sectors but fell about 7% in retail and hospitality. All five reversions came from retail/hospitality and healthcare administration." |
| "Revenue… 1.4% higher" | "Nominal revenue was 1.4% higher (52 of 61 organisations), which is likely a real-terms decline." |
| "Sick days fell 36%" | Add a seasonal caveat, or re-baseline against the same months of the prior year. |

## 7. Missing information that would most strengthen the paper

1. Actual hours, overtime and headcount changes, at least for the subsample that recorded them.
2. Organisation-level results with dispersion, and monthly output trajectories.
3. Real (inflation-adjusted) revenue, and an analysis restricted to organisations with objective output records.
4. Same-period prior-year baselines for sick days and resignations.
5. Survey response rates, and the characteristics of the nine withdrawn organisations and the nine missing revenue reports.
6. Customer-facing quality measures for retail and healthcare, such as service levels and customer satisfaction.

The paper's own recommendation for a comparison group is the right one. Until then, the evidence supports a narrower claim: reduced hours appear workable for self-selected knowledge-work organisations over six months, with weaker and less consistent results in customer-facing sectors.

I can redraft the Summary and Discussion along these lines if that would help.
